title: The Smartest Push Pull Legs Routine by Jeff Nippard review
summary: Cold read review of Jeff Nippard's 6-day leg-push-pull program. He praises the leg and push days, criticises the light pull days with their lat isolation and lack of leg and biceps work, and proposes fixes: hip hinges on pull days, supersets, more neck and biceps work, and a minimal 3-day version.
claims: He reviews programs cold without watching the video because most people run programs that way; a good program must stand on its own
A program that needs a whole book to be understood, as people say of Starting Strength, is simply a bad program
Leg-push-pull or pull-push-legs ordering beats push-pull-legs, especially with a rest day intercalated
Having two versions of each day adds variation and lowers overuse injury risk, but suits advanced lifters more than novices
He personally prefers to open his week with an upper day as preparation before lifting heavy with his legs
Squat 3x4 at 80% 1RM is good volume and intensity, though he would prefer evolving rep ranges
An almost perfect leg day starts with squats followed by Romanian deadlifts, covering knee flexion and hip hinge and about 80% of your bases
Eccentric leg extensions after squats, RDLs and leg press drift into junk volume and are not time efficient
Do not sit idle between sets; superset small muscle work (neck, forearms, shrugs) or pair leg press with leg curl and leg extension with calf raises, as waiting brings no hypertrophy benefit
End leg days with ab isolation: a stretch-focused move like decline crunches and a bracing move like long-lever planks
3x8 on bench invites much more sandbagging than 3x4 because of the extra reps
Upper body days should include two presses: one horizontal and one vertical
Dips at 3x12-15 after bench are fine within recovery; another horizontal press after that would be too much
Superset skullcrushers with dips and lateral raises with kickbacks; it costs nothing
The program lacks biceps work; add chin-ups on push day for biceps and upper back, since the upper back is gluttonous for volume
For deadlifts 3x3 is money and 1x5 is fine; 3x5 or 5x5 starts being too much volume
Bodybuilders should not neglect the deadlift: it puts mass on everything, covers the posterior chain and works the core
After deadlifts, use a knee flexion that spares the lower back, such as hack squats at 3x10-12
Rotate weekly: do single-leg hip thrusts for 4 sets of 10-15 one week, then replace them with the Nordic curl and back extension superset the next
Pull days should open with a hip hinge or a pull from the floor, not weighted pull-ups as strength work
Jeff's programs obsess over lat isolation; three lat exercises back to back is too much, spread them out
Training legs only twice in six days creates an imbalance; spread leg volume over more frequent sessions instead of crushing them
A better pull day: deadlift, weighted pull-ups, hack squats, then a giant set of cable rows, hip thrust or hamstring curl, calves and abs
He dislikes incline dumbbell curls; do chin-ups on another day instead
If you deadlifted heavy a day or two earlier, open the next leg day with pause squats at lower intensity for 6-10 reps instead of heavy 3x4 squats
Giving one leg day a knee-flexion emphasis and the other a hamstring emphasis is a good way to program
Overhead press 4x4 at 80% is slightly low volume but fine because intensity is high
Close-grip bench for 3x10 is his favorite rep range for that movement
The triceps long head is often forgotten in programs; overhead extensions give it the love it deserves
Neck work once every six days is not enough; do it more often, even at home
Shrugs can be superset anywhere in a program; it costs nothing
Curls should be mandatory, not optional, or you end up with massive triceps and no biceps
Biceps need intensity too: strict barbell curls for 3-4 sets of 3-6 reps will make them blow up
Open the second pull day with deficit or stiff-leg deadlifts, or standing rows that load legs and back, before pulldowns
Take the rest day after the pull day: three days on, one off
The program is extremely good and suits intermediates; for novices the volume and rotating variations are too much
Minimal version: leg day 1, push days 1 and 2 rotating, and leg day 2 used as pull day 1
exercises: covers hip hinge; with squats about 80% of leg needs
